Teaching

Neither English nor philosophy is just a body of knowledge to memorize. I teach both as tools for asking your own questions and thinking together with others.

What I value in class

Rather than memorizing correct answers, I emphasize clarifying the question, checking the evidence, building an argument and expressing it so that it reaches the reader or listener. Drawing on English-language teaching, critical thinking and philosophy education, I look for methods that let students keep learning on their own after the course ends.

Courses

I teach mainly in Academic Studies in English (ASE) at Tokyo Metropolitan University, including courses in English writing, discussion and presentation. ASE course offerings change from year to year; for current information, see the ASE website.

Generative AI and learning

With generative AI, I care less about whether to ban or allow it in class than about how to use it so that learning goes deeper. Instead of having AI produce answers, students and I try out ways of using it as a partner for reviewing their own writing and arguments and for broadening their thinking.

What matters most is telling apart what can be left to AI and what writers must take on themselves. What to ask, which evidence to trust and, in the end, what to claim are decisions the writer has to make.

On critical thinking

Critical thinking is not a technique for finding fault with others. It is a way of reading carefully: what is being claimed, what evidence supports it and what assumptions lie hidden. I aim to bring the methods of argument developed in philosophy into everyday settings such as writing, meetings, research and decision-making.

Now that generative AI returns plausible answers instantly, the ability to ask your own questions, judge how reliable information is and take responsibility for your own judgments matters more than ever.
